facts.statement: The study asks whether a chronic parasitic brain infection can protect mice from a lethal form of malaria.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: Mice lacking the gene for IL-33 still showed some protection against malaria, suggesting the protective mechanism is not entirely dependent on this specific molecule.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: Researchers measured brain cells and found that the chronic parasite infection changed astrocytes into a mixed type that showed both inflammatory and calming chemical markers.
facts.subject: cells_or_tissue

facts.statement: The study measured specific proteins in the brain and found that these changed astrocytes were a main source of IL-33 and helped attract a specific type of immune cell called ILC2s.
facts.subject: cells_or_tissue

facts.statement: The protection against malaria was linked to a specific pattern of gene activity in the brain that increased the production of TGF-beta and the IL-33/ST2 signaling pair.
facts.subject: animals
